lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: normal distributions, the empirical rule, and their limits
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: normal distributions, the empirical rule, and their limits

sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: Read the example first. You are not expected to know this yet.

items.prompt: Mean 100, sd 15. What percentage lies between 70 and 130?

steps: That is 100 ± 30, which is two standard deviations.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Try each one. If you get stuck, write what you do know and move on.

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 48%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±48%, giving 0% to 96%
±10%, giving 38% to 58%
±5%, giving 43% to 53%

items.prompt: In 1000 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 6 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 0.6% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 0.6% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 67 and standard deviation 4. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 59 and 75?
choices: about 50%
about 99.7%
about 68%
about 95%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a sample survey with randomly selected participants. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.

sections.title: Mastery check
sections.directions: Show what you can do so far. This sets the starting point, not a grade.

items.prompt: A random sample of 400 people gives a sample proportion of 59%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±5%, giving 54% to 64%
±59%, giving 0% to 118%
±10%, giving 49% to 69%

items.prompt: In 500 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 13 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 2.6% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 2.6% of simulations, which is not unusual.
